analysis.one_liner: Makes the EB-5 foreign-investor visa program for regional centers permanent and streamlines its processing.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; introduced with zero cosponsors in December 2007, it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The EB-5 program lets foreigners get U.S. green cards by investing in projects that create American jobs. Since 1993 a slice of it, the "regional center" program, has only been authorized temporarily, requiring Congress to keep renewing it. This bill would strike that time limit, making the program permanent. It would also let applicants file their petition and green-card application at the same time to speed things up, charge investors a $2,000 fee for faster processing, charge regional centers a $2,500 application fee, and use those fees to fund the program's administration.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy foreign investors, who would gain a permanent, faster route to U.S. residency, and the regional centers — development and investment funds that pool foreign money into U.S. projects — whose business model would no longer depend on Congress renewing the program every few years. U.S. workers hired by funded projects would get some indirect benefit through the investment the program attracts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy foreign investors and regional-center funds

how_it_helps.text: Removes the 15-year sunset on the EB-5 regional center program, making it permanent rather than subject to repeated congressional renewals.
Allows EB-5 investors to file their immigrant petition and adjustment-of-status application at the same time when a visa is immediately available, cutting waiting time.
Creates a $2,000 premium processing fee for EB-5 petitions and a $2,500 regional center designation fee, with the money dedicated to administering the EB-5 program.

analysis.who_pays: The program's participants: investors pay a $2,000 premium processing fee and regional centers pay a $2,500 designation fee, which would presumably be passed along in project costs. Taxpayers would bear little direct cost, since the bill funds the program's administration out of these new fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: EB-5 investors and regional centers, via fees

drawbacks.text: By striking the sunset provision, the bill would permanently entrench a visa pathway that, by design, offers residency based on wealth, a policy choice Congress could otherwise revisit each time the program comes up for renewal.

The bill's practical benefits are narrow: it changes processing mechanics and fees for one small immigration category and creates no new visas, so its effect on ordinary people's lives is modest at best.
The new fees would raise the cost of participating in the program for investors and regional centers, costs likely to be reflected in investment offerings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest, fee-funded housekeeping measure for a niche immigration program: it speeds processing and makes the program permanent while covering its own administrative costs. The main trade-off is that permanence locks in a residency-by-investment pathway that Congress would otherwise periodically have to affirmatively renew, and the bill creates nothing new for anyone outside the program. It drew no cosponsors and no recorded committee action, suggesting few colleagues saw urgency in it either way.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Flake introduced the bill on December 19, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
On January 14, 2008, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where it remained.
No further action was taken; the bill died at the end of the 110th Congress without a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much from the bill's death; the status quo prevailed, meaning the regional center program stayed temporary and continued operating only under periodic congressional extensions. The main beneficiaries of the outcome are anyone who preferred Congress retain the ability to reconsider the program's terms each cycle.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; the program stayed temporary

for.name: Rep. Jeff Flake
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the EB-5 regional center program permanent and streamline its processing.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired by Rep. John Conyers, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security on January 14, 2008, and took no further action on it — no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no votes were ever recorded, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: EB-5 regional centers (investment funds and development projects that pool foreign money)
industries.note: Making the program permanent would remove the periodic risk that Congress lets their authorization lapse, locking in their role as the channel through which foreigners buy into U.S. residency via investment. The bill would also charge centers a $2,500 application fee and fund program administration through fees. The public connection runs through jobs created by funded projects — the program's premise — while residency itself goes to wealthy foreigners.

industries.industry: Wealthy foreign investors seeking U.S. residency
industries.note: Investors would gain a permanent program, a $2,000 fast-track processing option, and the ability to file their green-card application concurrently with their petition. The program's premise is that their investment creates U.S. jobs, tying their gain to some public benefit.
